reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Measured adoption of AI in educational services sits at 30.0% of firms, according to the Census Bureau, which asks whether a business used AI in the last two weeks. The same series shows a prior period figure of 35.5%, so the most recent reading is lower than the one before it. The Census Bureau notes that an S marks suppressed values in this series, and the question was first asked in September 2023. That is the only hard adoption number the material offers for the sector, and it covers firms classified under NAICS 61.

On the policy side, the Department of Education has issued federal AI guidance covering innovation and risk management, and it maintains an inventory of its own AI use cases. The uses it lists are operational rather than instructional: CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics and intelligent automation, Grammarly for written communication, Otter.AI for transcription and meeting collaboration, and AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models. The Department also describes generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in multiple programming languages, extracting key points and action items from public documents, generating R code for data analysis, training employees on prompt engineering, automating conversion between data types such as mapping a county name to its FIPS code, generating mock datasets for testing, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, testing filters against fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information, and suggesting descriptive paragraphs, workflow diagrams and qualifications for public positions. The guidance frames this work as adherence to federal regulation and to an executive order on American leadership in AI.

Market intelligence on the education economy comes from HolonIQ, which describes itself as a platform for impact market intelligence. It reports on sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, scoring impact through rubrics and ratings, mapping partnership landscapes and tracking alliances, and mapping competitive landscapes. HolonIQ says it serves governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms and investors, and that global media rely on it for data on the impact economy. It does not publish specific adoption or spending figures in the material available here.

This site's own cataloguing work covers AI courses and credentials. It lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, each curated by level and audience with one verified source and re-verified daily. The catalogued providers include DeepLearning.AI on Coursera, Dataquest, fast.ai, DeepLearning.AI with Stanford, Google, Hugging Face, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry. The site notes that university courses tend to be structured around exam-driven theory while the industry courses are described as code-first or hands-on, so the choice is about how someone wants to learn rather than which source is more rigorous. It also states plainly that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

The sourced points add that the education sections track the courses and credentials the field actually uses, with costs and renewal cycles pointing at issuer pages, and that HolonIQ covers EdTech funding, digital transformation and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed and workforce learning. The page's stated scope is tutoring systems, drafting assistance and academic integrity policy from K-12 through university, alongside market tracking and the course catalog.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few cautious takeaways. The Census Bureau figure gives a sector-level adoption rate with a recent decline, not a forecast. The Department of Education guidance shows what a federal education agency considers permissible and how it documents its own use cases, which is the closest thing here to a regulatory posture. HolonIQ describes the market-intelligence layer without publishing numbers in this material. The course catalog speaks to where skills are being taught rather than where institutions are buying. Nothing in the sources reports ROI, vendor concentration or spending levels for education specifically, so those questions remain open on this evidence.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
